summary: A Live Science article by Christopher Wanjek, published 28 September 2016, reports a Nature study led by José María Gómez of Spain's CSIC finding that primates, including humans, kill members of their own species nearly six times more often than the average mammal. The study analyzed deaths across 1,024 mammal species and about 600 human populations, finding that about 2 percent of human deaths come from interpersonal violence, similar to other primates. Experts quoted note that human violence has fluctuated historically and that data limitations exist, while Gómez suggests sociality and territoriality drive lethal violence.
one_line: A 2016 Nature study finds primates, including humans, commit lethal within-species violence far more often than average mammals.
key_facts: Primates kill within their own species nearly six times more often than the average mammal, according to Spanish researchers.
The study was published on 28 September 2016 in the journal Nature.
The study was led by José María Gómez of Spain's Higher Council for Scientific Research (CSIC).
The researchers analyzed data from more than 4 million deaths among members of 1,024 mammal species from 137 taxonomic families.
The data included about 600 human populations, ranging from about 50,000 years ago to the present.
About 2 percent of all human deaths have been caused by interpersonal violence, a figure matching observed values for prehistoric humans such as Neanderthals and most other primates.
Whales rarely kill each other; the same goes for bats and rabbits, according to the article.
Levels of lethal interpersonal human violence have fluctuated throughout history, from low levels during nomadic periods to higher levels when plunder and conquest became profitable.
The researchers said human culture can influence our evolutionarily inherited level of lethal violence.
Douglas Fry, professor and chair of anthropology at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, said the study debunks the old 'killer ape' view of humanity.
Richard Wrangham, a professor of biological anthropology at Harvard University, said humans 'really are exceptional' in lethal violence and suspects humans are more violent than the study suggests.
Gómez said: 'Within primates, humans are not unusually violent.'
Gómez said: 'Territorial and social species showed significantly higher values of lethal violence than solitary and nonterritorial mammals.'
Wrangham noted an inherent underestimation of violent death in prehistoric humans given the lack of forensic evidence.
